http_response.description: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. http_response.description: 27-year-old man with 2-year history of recurrent convulsions. Episodes began with shaking of the trunk, arms, and legs lasting 4–5 minutes, sometimes preceded by occipital pain radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. data.description: Congenital true diverticulum of the distal ileum that may contain ectopic gastric mucosa, leading to painless lower GI bleeding; can also act as a lead point for intussusception, adding colicky pain.
symptoms_in_common: Age and male sex consistent with typical presentation
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent severe colicky abdominal pain with leg-drawing (Meckel bleeding alone is often painless; pain suggests complications such as intussusception or inflammation)
Episodes of abdominal rigidity
Hemodynamic compromise (less typical unless bleeding is massive or there is associated ischemia)

data.description: Torsion of the intestine around a narrow mesenteric base in malrotation, leading to bowel ischemia, severe pain, and potentially hematochezia and shock.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent severe abdominal pain with rigidity
Progressive hematochezia with large clot (possible with ischemia)
Diffuse tenderness worse on the right
Pallor, tachycardia, and lower blood pressure suggesting compromised perfusion
symptoms_not_in_common: Lack of reported bilious vomiting (classically present in volvulus)
No palpable abdominal mass (not expected but sometimes present with other causes)
No prior history suggesting malrotation (often silent until acute event)

data.diagnosis: Allergic proctocolitis (cow’s milk protein induced colitis)
data.description: Inflammatory reaction of the distal colon in infants to dietary proteins (often cow’s milk/soy), causing blood-streaked stools in otherwise well infants.
symptoms_in_common: Exposure to cow’s milk-based formula and recent dietary changes (pureed foods)
symptoms_not_in_common: Large-volume bleeding with a large clot (typically bleeding is mild)
Intermittent severe colicky pain and abdominal rigidity (usually minimal discomfort)
Diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right
Pallor, tachycardia, and lower blood pressure (hemodynamic instability is not typical)

data.description: Bacterial infection of the colon causing inflammatory diarrhea with abdominal pain and hematochezia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent nocturnal colicky pain with leg-drawing (pain in infectious colitis is typically more continuous and associated with diarrhea/tenesmus)
Episodes of abdominal rigidity
Large clot in stool (clots are less typical than bloody diarrhea)
Hemodynamic compromise (possible but less typical without severe dehydration or sepsis)

data.diagnosis: Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) with gastrointestinal involvement
data.description: Small-vessel IgA-mediated vasculitis in children that can cause colicky abdominal pain, GI bleeding, and potential intussusception in addition to purpuric rash and arthralgias.
symptoms_not_in_common: Episodes of abdominal rigidity (not classic without severe complications)
Hemodynamic instability (uncommon unless severe GI involvement/bleeding)
Lack of other typical systemic features noted such as purpuric rash or arthralgias is not documented as present

http_response.description: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

data.description: A small-airways disease characterized by inflammation and fibrosis leading to luminal narrowing and airflow obstruction; often presents with progressive dyspnea and obstructive spirometry with minimal reversibility.
symptoms_in_common: Severely reduced FEV1 (32% predicted) indicating severe obstruction
Flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease
Normal echocardiogram reducing likelihood of a cardiac cause
symptoms_not_in_common: No relevant past medical or drug history (many cases are secondary to exposures, drugs, autoimmune disease, or transplant)

data.description: Chronic inflammatory airway disease causing variable airflow limitation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness; can present de novo in older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Severely reduced FEV1 compatible with obstructive physiology
Flow-volume loop consistent with small airways obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Lack of documented bronchodilator reversibility (not reported)
No history of atopy, wheeze, or triggers reported
New presentation at age 69 is less typical though possible

data.diagnosis: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in a non-smoker
data.description: Persistent airflow limitation due to airway/alveolar abnormalities; typically from smoking but can result from biomass exposure, occupational exposures, or prior severe infections.
symptoms_in_common: Small airway involvement suggested by flow-volume loop
symptoms_not_in_common: Non-smoker (most COPD cases are smoking-related)
No chronic cough or sputum production reported
No known exposure history provided (biomass/occupational)

data.description: Immune-mediated lung disease due to inhaled antigens causing small-airway inflammation; can present with dyspnea and mixed or obstructive physiology, especially in chronic forms.
symptoms_in_common: Small airway disease suggested by flow-volume loop
Obstructive impairment on spirometry can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No exposure history reported (birds, molds, occupational antigens)
No systemic symptoms (fever, malaise) reported
No cough reported (often present)

data.description: Genetic deficiency leading to panacinar emphysema and airflow obstruction, often in non-smokers or with minimal smoking; classically lower-lobe predominant.
symptoms_in_common: Severe airflow obstruction with markedly reduced FEV1
symptoms_not_in_common: Late age of presentation (often presents earlier)
No personal or family history of liver disease or early-onset emphysema reported

data.description: Chronic inflammatory small-airways disease characterized by diffuse involvement of respiratory bronchioles; classically seen in East Asian populations with chronic sinusitis and obstructive physiology.
symptoms_in_common: Small airway disease pattern on flow-volume loop
symptoms_not_in_common: No chronic productive cough reported
No chronic rhinosinusitis reported
No mention of East Asian ancestry (classically associated)

http_response.description: 27-year-old man with a few days of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. History notable for left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement that had fluctuated since age 15. On examination, he was thin, with low-grade fever, mild hypoxemia, left upper lung crackles, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures were negative, as were serologies for ANCA, rheumatoid factor, HIV, and tumor markers. Otologic evaluation was unremarkable. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identified pathogens.

data.description: A multisystem granulomatous disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most commonly affecting the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes, and often associated with elevated soluble IL-2 receptor.
symptoms_in_common: Transbronchial lung biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation without identified pathogens
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemoptysis (less typical in sarcoidosis)
Leukocytosis with neutrophilia (sarcoidosis more often has lymphopenia)
Longstanding solitary supraclavicular node since adolescence (sarcoidosis more typically causes bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy)

data.description: Mycobacterial infection that commonly involves the lungs, causing caseating granulomas; classic symptoms include chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, fever, and hemoptysis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative sputum and blood cultures
Absence of weight loss and night sweats
Granulomas without identified pathogens and without caseation reported
Elevated soluble IL-2 receptor (not typical for TB)
Longstanding fluctuating supraclavicular node since adolescence (does not fit typical natural history of TB)

data.description: A necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis affecting small to medium vessels, commonly involving the upper and lower respiratory tracts and kidneys; hemoptysis can occur with pulmonary involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: ANCA serology negative (many cases are ANCA-positive, though ANCA-negative disease exists)
Lack of upper airway (sinus, otologic) involvement
No renal findings reported
Longstanding isolated supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (lymph node enlargement is not a typical hallmark)

data.description: Immune-mediated interstitial lung disease due to inhaled antigens, characterized by poorly formed noncaseating granulomas, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemoptysis (uncommon in hypersensitivity pneumonitis)
No known exposure history provided
Longstanding supraclavicular lymphadenopathy since adolescence (not characteristic)
Elevated soluble IL-2 receptor (not typical)

data.diagnosis: Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvement or sarcoid-like reaction
data.description: A lymphoid malignancy characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells and classically presenting with painless, rubbery lymphadenopathy; can occasionally involve the lungs or provoke sarcoid-like granulomatous reactions.
symptoms_in_common: Firm, rubbery, nontender supraclavicular lymph node
symptoms_not_in_common: Granulomatous inflammation on lung biopsy without malignant cells (Hodgkin lymphoma typically shows Reed-Sternberg cells; granulomas suggest sarcoid-like reaction rather than direct lymphoma)
Hemoptysis is uncommon in Hodgkin lymphoma
Leukocytosis with neutrophilia (HL more often shows lymphocyte abnormalities)
Acute onset over a few days (HL symptoms usually more subacute/chronic)

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary histoplasmosis (or other endemic fungal granulomatous infection)
data.description: Infection by Histoplasma capsulatum (or similar fungi), causing pulmonary granulomas and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; presentations range from asymptomatic to subacute pulmonary disease with cough and fever.
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemoptysis is less typical in uncomplicated histoplasmosis
No geographic or exposure history provided
Longstanding supraclavicular lymph node since adolescence (not characteristic)
Elevated soluble IL-2 receptor (not typical for fungal infection)
Lack of organism identification on special stains/cultures

http_response.description: A 31-year-old Caucasian man with multiple sclerosis who had received 24 natalizumab infusions and was switched to fingolimod due to persistent high anti-JCPyV antibody index (3.61). After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs. He presented with leukopenia (0.83 × 10^9/L) at hospital admission.

data.diagnosis: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC virus
data.description: Opportunistic demyelinating disease caused by JC virus reactivation in the setting of immunosuppression, strongly associated with natalizumab exposure and high anti-JC virus antibody index.
symptoms_in_common: Nystagmus and other focal neurological signs
History of multiple sclerosis treated with natalizumab and recent switch to fingolimod
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked leukopenia (more a treatment effect than a typical PML manifestation)
Distal tremor and upper-limb spasm (can occur but are less typical presenting features)

data.description: Paradoxical inflammatory worsening of PML lesions due to immune reconstitution after withdrawal of natalizumab; can occur within weeks to months after stopping natalizumab, sometimes even when switched to another agent.
symptoms_in_common: Acute/subacute neurological deterioration after stopping natalizumab
Homonymous hemianopia and other focal deficits
symptoms_not_in_common: Current immunosuppression with fingolimod (tends to blunt IRIS rather than promote it)
Leukopenia (not typical of IRIS; IRIS usually occurs with immune recovery, not cytopenia)
Distal tremor and upper-limb spasm (less typical as primary manifestations)

data.description: Reversible vasogenic edema of the posterior circulation often triggered by cytotoxic/immunosuppressive drugs, hypertension, or renal failure; presents with seizures and visual disturbances.
symptoms_in_common: Recent exposure to immunomodulatory therapy (fingolimod/natalizumab) which has been rarely associated with PRES
symptoms_not_in_common: Leukopenia (not a typical PRES feature)
Lateral nystagmus (not classic for PRES, though visual disturbances are common)
Distal tremor and upper-limb spasm (not characteristic)
No reported severe hypertension or headache (common in PRES but not described)

data.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis relapse with occipital/cortical involvement
data.description: An acute demyelinating relapse affecting visual pathways and cortical regions in a patient with MS, potentially leading to visual field deficits and, less commonly, seizures.
symptoms_in_common: Seizures (uncommon but possible in MS with cortical involvement)
symptoms_not_in_common: Leukopenia (not explained by an MS relapse; more consistent with drug effect)
Recent high-risk JC virus status and prior natalizumab exposure (raise concern for PML rather than typical MS relapse)

data.diagnosis: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) with occipital involvement
data.description: Thrombosis of cerebral venous sinuses leading to venous congestion, infarction, and seizures; can cause visual field defects if occipital lobes are involved.
symptoms_not_in_common: Leukopenia (not typical for CVST)
Lateral nystagmus and distal tremor/spasm (not characteristic)
No reported headache or papilledema (commonly seen in CVST)
Immunosuppressive therapy history (not a usual CVST risk factor)

http_response.description: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

data.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A (GLA) activity leading to globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) accumulation, with neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, cornea verticillata, renal and cardiac involvement, and auditory/vestibular symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Burning neuropathic pain in extremities since childhood
Intermittent atypical chest discomfort (possible cardiac involvement)
Markedly reduced plasma alpha-galactosidase A activity
Pathogenic hemizygous GLA mutation (exon 4 c.617T>C, p.Leu206Pro)

data.description: A hereditary nephropathy due to mutations in type IV collagen (COL4A3/A4/A5) characterized by progressive renal disease with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities (e.g., anterior lenticonus, dot-and-fleck retinopathy).
symptoms_not_in_common: Angiokeratomas on trunk
Cornea verticillata
Burning neuropathic pain since childhood
Intermittent atypical chest discomfort related to storage cardiomyopathy
Markedly reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity
GLA mutation confirming lysosomal enzyme deficiency
Absence of hematuria (typically present in Alport)

data.description: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of alpha-L-fucosidase, leading to accumulation of fucose-containing glycoproteins and glycolipids; features can include developmental delay, coarse facies, angiokeratomas, recurrent infections, and neurologic involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Cornea verticillata (not typical)
Proteinuria without hematuria (renal involvement is not classic and differs)
Intermittent atypical chest discomfort
Markedly reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity (would not be expected; enzyme defect is different)
Presence of pathogenic GLA mutation (not expected in fucosidosis)
Onset with isolated neuropathic pain without developmental delay or coarse facies

data.diagnosis: Schindler disease type 2 (Kanzaki disease; alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase deficiency)
data.description: A rare lysosomal storage disorder characterized by deficiency of alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase leading to angiokeratomas, peripheral neuropathy, and sometimes hearing loss; typically adult-onset with dermatologic findings.
symptoms_not_in_common: Cornea verticillata
Proteinuria without hematuria
Intermittent atypical chest discomfort
Markedly reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity (enzyme defect is different)
Confirmed GLA mutation (not expected in Kanzaki disease)

data.description: A peripheral neuropathy affecting small unmyelinated fibers, causing burning pain, dysesthesias, and autonomic symptoms; etiologies include diabetes, autoimmune, toxins, or idiopathic.
symptoms_in_common: Burning neuropathic pain in extremities (since childhood)
symptoms_not_in_common: Angiokeratomas on trunk
Cornea verticillata
Proteinuria without hematuria
Tinnitus
Intermittent atypical chest discomfort related to storage disease
Markedly reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity
Presence of GLA pathogenic variant

http_response.description: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.

data.description: Bacterial superinfection of a pre-existing intrahepatic hematoma leading to a hepatic abscess, common in trauma patients and presents with systemic signs of infection and liver test abnormalities.

history of intrahepatic hematoma

history of intrahepatic hematoma

data.description: Liver injury caused by medications (e.g., antibiotics, antiepileptics, parenteral nutrition) commonly used in ICU; may present with fever, leukocytosis (if hypersensitivity), and elevated liver enzymes.

history of intrahepatic hematoma

data.description: Hepatocellular injury due to hepatic hypoperfusion, often in the setting of shock or severe hypotension; characterized by markedly elevated transaminases more than cholestatic enzymes; fever is not a core feature.

symptoms_not_in_common: fever
leukocytosis
onset during ICU hospitalization (day 7) without documented hypotension
history of intrahepatic hematoma

http_response.description: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

data.description: A severe, acute pustular drug reaction characterized by sudden onset of numerous sterile, non-follicular pustules on an erythematous base, often within hours to a few days after exposure to a culprit medication (including iodinated contrast), accompanied by neutrophilia and sometimes eosinophilia; typically resolves after withdrawal of the trigger.
symptoms_in_common: Onset within hours after iodinated contrast exposure
Generalized sterile pustular eruption with coalescing pustules on trunk and extremities
Presence of vesicles/bullae over erythematous skin
Diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis (more typical of SJS/TEN than AGEP)
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia (not classic for AGEP)
Hematuria (not a typical AGEP manifestation)

data.description: A severe mucocutaneous drug reaction characterized by extensive keratinocyte apoptosis leading to full-thickness epidermal necrosis and detachment; usually occurs 1–3 weeks after drug initiation and often involves mucous membranes; may be triggered by various drugs including contrast media.
symptoms_in_common: Temporal relationship to a drug exposure (iodinated contrast)
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset within hours (SJS/TEN typically has a longer latency)
Prominent sterile pustules and pus-filled bullae (not typical for SJS/TEN)
Diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate (SJS/TEN more often shows sparse inflammatory infiltrate)
Mild eosinophilia (not characteristic)
Lack of reported mucosal involvement
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia (not typical for SJS/TEN)
Hematuria (not a defining feature)

data.description: An acute, potentially life-threatening form of psoriasis characterized by widespread pustules on erythematous skin, systemic inflammation, and neutrophilia; may be triggered by drugs, infections, or withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids.
symptoms_in_common: Generalized coalescing sterile pustules on trunk and limbs
Pus-filled lesions that may form lakes of pus
symptoms_not_in_common: Full-thickness epidermal necrosis (not typical; histology usually shows spongiform pustules of Kogoj)
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia (not classic)
Onset within hours after a single exposure (GPP often has variable course and triggers)
Mild eosinophilia (not typical)
No history of psoriasis reported
Hematuria (unrelated)

data.diagnosis: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), drug-induced
data.description: An acute neutrophilic dermatosis presenting with tender, erythematous plaques and a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in the dermis, often associated with fever and leukocytosis; can be triggered by medications and less commonly presents with vesiculopustular or bullous lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly pustular and bullous eruption rather than typical tender plaques
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis (not characteristic)

She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. 45-year-old man with acute illness after dog bites. He developed nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting the day before admission. Three days earlier, he had been bitten on the hands and forearms while bathing his dog; he also had head trauma from a rusty nail a few days earlier and dental extractions 1–2 weeks earlier. Past history included asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse with heavy recent intake. On exam, he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic with hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and elevated blood pressure. He had multiple lacerations with necrotic edges and scratch marks on the hands and forearms, including a 3–4 cm right forearm lesion with a 5–7 cm surrounding purplish border, and capillary refill of 5 seconds.

data.description: A severe, rapidly progressive sepsis caused by Capnocytophaga species commonly found in the oral flora of dogs; high risk in people with alcohol use disorder, cirrhosis, or asplenia after dog bites or scratches.
symptoms_in_common: Recent dog bites/scratches to hands and forearms
Ill-appearing with systemic toxicity (tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis)
Skin lesions with necrotic edges and purplish discoloration
Prolonged capillary refill (suggestive of poor perfusion/shock)
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated blood pressure (sepsis often causes hypotension later)
Epigastric pain and vomiting (not specific to Capnocytophaga; could be concurrent or due to alcohol)

data.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissues often caused by polymicrobial flora or group A Streptococcus, sometimes following traumatic wounds or animal bites.
symptoms_in_common: Recent traumatic dog bite wounds to forearms/hands
Skin lesions with necrotic edges and violaceous/purplish borders
Prolonged capillary refill indicating poor perfusion
symptoms_not_in_common: No report of severe pain out of proportion to exam (classic feature)
No crepitus or bullae reported
Elevated blood pressure (often hypotension/shock develops)

data.diagnosis: Pasteurella multocida cellulitis with possible bacteremia
data.description: A common rapidly developing soft tissue infection following dog or cat bites caused by Pasteurella species; can progress to systemic illness, especially in high-risk hosts.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid onset local infection with necrotic-appearing edges
Prolonged capillary refill suggesting systemic compromise
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypothermia (fever more typical early)
Purplish border/necrosis more suggestive of necrotizing infection or sepsis-associated purpura
Significant nausea, epigastric pain, vomiting (non-specific)

data.description: A fulminant soft tissue infection due to Clostridium species causing muscle necrosis, systemic toxicity, and potentially crepitus; can follow traumatic wounds contaminated with soil or devitalized tissue.

symptoms_not_in_common: No crepitus reported
Location on forearm from dog bites (classically associated with deep traumatic or crush injuries)
No mention of foul-smelling discharge
Elevated blood pressure (often hypotension with progression)

Prominent local necrosis with purplish border (not characteristic of tetanus)

Acute onset within a few days (tetanus usually has longer incubation)

http_response.description: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

data.diagnosis: MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes)

symptoms_in_common: Childhood-onset muscle weakness and gait disturbance
Decreased muscle tone and atrophic muscle mass
Muscle biopsy consistent with mitochondrial myopathy
Stroke-like episodes with aphasia, dysarthria, and hemiplegia

Laboratory hyperthyroidism (low TSH, high free T4)

Documented MT-TL1 mitochondrial mutation

Right-sided chest pain
Yellow-white sputum (asthma cough often non-productive)
Lack of documented wheezing or variable airflow limitation on exam

Right-sided chest pain
No reported nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, or throat clearing

Normal temperature and clear percussion notes

http_response.description: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

Exposure to forests/islands in a Mediterranean region (mosquito exposure)

symptoms_not_in_common: Lack of known ingestion of contaminated water/raw amphibian or reptile meat
Normal eosinophil count and inflammatory markers
Ultrasound appearing normal rather than tubular/track-like lesion
Sparganosis is rare in Croatia compared to Dirofilaria

Exposure history (dogs/forests) not relevant to lipoma

Lack of typical central punctum or episodes of inflammation
Multiple migrating nodules reported rather than a single stationary lesion

data.description: Zoonotic nematode infection acquired by ingesting raw/undercooked fish or contaminated water; causes intermittent, migrating subcutaneous swellings and eosinophilia; more common in Asia and Latin America.
symptoms_in_common: Painless or mildly tender subcutaneous swelling
Normal systemic inflammatory markers can occur

No history of eating raw/undercooked freshwater fish or contaminated water reported
Normal eosinophil count (eosinophilia is common)
Ultrasound unremarkable (lesions may show tracks or edema)

data.description: A benign, rapidly growing myofibroblastic proliferation in the subcutis or fascia; presents as a firm nodule, often on the upper extremities; can be mistaken for sarcoma but is self-limited.
symptoms_not_in_common: Migration of the nodule (nodular fasciitis is typically fixed in place)
Multiple migrating nodules rather than a single rapidly growing lesion
Exposure to dogs/forests not relevant
Ultrasound often shows a solid lesion rather than completely normal appearance

http_response.description: 66-year-old man with progressive gait instability and frequent falls since around 2000, followed by blurred vision, photophobia, and worsening imbalance from 2003. He had bilateral cataract surgery with lens implantation in 2000 without benefit. Over time he developed slurred speech, inability to look down, dysphagia with repeated aspirations, and increasing postural instability requiring a cane. On examination he had irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes, severe impairment of voluntary vertical gaze, slowed horizontal pursuit with bilateral adduction paresis, preserved convergence early on, later absent vertical and medial eye movements, no Bell’s phenomenon, no optokinetic or caloric-induced nystagmus, and absent doll’s eye movements. He also had severe nuchal rigidity, retrocollis, axial rigidity, inability to sit independently, backward falls, and no resting tremor.

data.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by early postural instability with backward falls, axial rigidity, dysarthria/dysphagia, and a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy due to midbrain dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive gait instability with frequent backward falls
Severe impairment of voluntary vertical gaze (inability to look down)
Slowed horizontal pursuit and bilateral adduction paresis
Absent doll’s eye movements (impaired vestibulo-ocular reflex)
Axial rigidity with retrocollis and severe nuchal rigidity
Inability to sit independently (severe postural instability)
Photophobia and blurred vision related to supranuclear ophthalmoplegia
symptoms_not_in_common: Irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes (can occur but are less emphasized in classic PSP)
History of cataract surgery without benefit (not a defining feature)

data.description: A synucleinopathy presenting with bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, and postural instability; typical ocular movements are preserved except for hypometric saccades in later stages.

symptoms_not_in_common: Early severe backward falls
Severe supranuclear vertical gaze palsy and horizontal pursuit slowing
Absent doll’s eye movements and OKN/caloric responses
Retrocollis and severe nuchal rigidity
No resting tremor (tremor often present in PD)
Lack of clear bradykinesia description
Photophobia and prominent ophthalmoplegia

data.description: A rapidly progressive synucleinopathy with parkinsonism poorly responsive to levodopa, autonomic failure, and sometimes cerebellar signs; ocular findings typically include saccadic abnormalities but not marked vertical supranuclear palsy.
symptoms_in_common: Possible retrocollis (can be seen in MSA)
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe supranuclear vertical gaze palsy and absent VOR
No reported autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, urinary/erectile dysfunction) which is typical of MSA
Marked absence of cerebellar signs (e.g., limb ataxia) despite long course
Photophobia and profound ophthalmoplegia are atypical for MSA

data.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy with asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, dystonia, myoclonus, and cortical signs; ocular motor abnormalities can occur but profound vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is less typical than in PSP.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with absent VOR (more characteristic of PSP)
Symmetric axial predominance without reported asymmetric limb findings
Lack of cortical features such as limb apraxia, alien limb phenomenon, cortical sensory loss, or myoclonus
Retrocollis and severe nuchal rigidity are unusual for corticobasal syndrome

data.diagnosis: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome due to structural midbrain pathology
data.description: A syndrome from lesions of the dorsal midbrain (e.g., tumor, stroke, MS) causing vertical gaze palsy, light-near dissociation of pupils, and convergence abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to look down and severe impairment of voluntary vertical gaze
Irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes (suggesting light-near dissociation)
Slowed horizontal pursuit and adduction paresis
symptoms_not_in_common: Long progressive course over decades (structural Parinaud is often acute/subacute)
Severe axial rigidity, retrocollis, and backward falls
Dysarthria and dysphagia with repeated aspirations
Absent doll’s eye movements and global vestibulo-ocular failure
No Bell’s phenomenon
Lack of other focal signs suggestive of a discrete structural lesion

http_response.description: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. data.description: An opportunistic fungal infection causing subacute to chronic meningitis, classically in patients with advanced AIDS; characterized by high opening pressure and lymphocytic CSF.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute 2-week course of headache and fever
Advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 7 cells/µL, high viral load)

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the meninges causing subacute meningitis; common in immunocompromised patients; often shows lymphocytic CSF with high protein and low glucose.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute 2-week history of fever and headache
symptoms_not_in_common: Photophobia (can occur but is less emphasized compared to other meningitides)

data.description: Herpes simplex virus type 2 can cause a benign recurrent or primary aseptic meningitis with lymphocytic CSF, typically in sexually active adults.

Markedly elevated opening pressure (less characteristic for CMV)

http_response.description: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) due to ischemic stroke (medial longitudinal fasciculus infarct)

symptoms_in_common: inability to adduct the left eye
abducting (gaze-evoked) nystagmus in the right eye on attempted left gaze
symptoms_not_in_common: diplopia only when looking through the right eye (monocular diplopia is atypical for INO, which usually causes binocular diplopia)

data.description: An acute ischemic event in the vertebrobasilar territory affecting brainstem structures, which can produce isolated ocular motor abnormalities such as INO with minimal additional deficits.

abducting nystagmus in the right eye
otherwise normal neurological examination (possible isolated ocular motor stroke)
symptoms_not_in_common: monocular diplopia reported through the right eye (posterior circulation strokes typically cause binocular diplopia)
absence of other posterior circulation signs (e.g., ataxia, dysarthria, weakness), though isolated presentations can occur

data.description: Microvascular ischemia of the oculomotor nerve, often due to vascular risk factors, leading to deficits in adduction, elevation, and depression, sometimes with ptosis and pupil sparing.

vascular risk profile (elderly with atrial fibrillation)
symptoms_not_in_common: abducting nystagmus in the right eye (not typical of isolated CN III palsy)
lack of ptosis

monocular diplopia description (CN III palsy typically causes binocular diplopia)

no ptosis reported

advanced age (risk for cataract and corneal changes)

http_response.description: 27-year-old man with 3 days of progressive myalgias in the thighs followed by acute weakness of the legs and arms on the day of presentation, unable to lift his legs or stand. http_response.description: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

http_response.description: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

symptoms_not_in_common: Muscle weakness and myalgia (not typical of PCT)
Intermittent fever (not typical)
Impaired 'prayer sign' (not a feature of PCT)
Positive ANA (not characteristic)
Rash distribution on trunk and extremities without mention of blistering/skin fragility

data.description: Autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by skin thickening and contractures (sclerodactyly) that can impair the 'prayer sign,' sometimes overlapping with inflammatory myopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Muscle weakness and pain (possible overlap myositis)
symptoms_not_in_common: Photosensitive rash (not typical for systemic sclerosis)
Intermittent fever (less typical)
Cholestatic liver enzyme elevation without clear biliary disease
Post–stem cell transplant context (makes cGVHD more likely than primary systemic sclerosis)

http_response.description: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

data.diagnosis: Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle disease/perforating folliculitis) associated with end-stage renal disease
data.description: A group of perforating disorders seen commonly in patients with chronic kidney disease (and diabetes) characterized by intensely pruritic, umbilicated papules or nodules with a central keratin plug on extensor surfaces; lesions often arise or are exacerbated by scratching (Koebner phenomenon).
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominant restriction to sun-exposed areas (classically not purely photodistributed)

data.diagnosis: Prurigo nodularis secondary to chronic kidney disease (uremic prurigo)
data.description: A chronic, intensely itchy dermatosis with multiple hyperkeratotic nodules that arises from repeated scratching; commonly associated with systemic pruritic conditions such as chronic kidney disease and can severely impair sleep and quality of life.
symptoms_not_in_common: Photodistribution (lesions limited to sun-exposed areas is less typical; PN usually relates more to scratching patterns than sun exposure)

data.description: A common idiopathic photodermatosis characterized by pruritic papules, papulovesicles, or plaques occurring hours to days after sun exposure on sun-exposed skin, often recurring seasonally.
symptoms_in_common: Distribution on sun-exposed areas of the extremities
No history of habitual UV-light exposure (PMLE can occur with ordinary incidental sun exposure)
symptoms_not_in_common: Male sex and age 51 years (PMLE is more common in younger women)
Prolonged continuous course over 10 months without clear seasonal pattern
Underlying severe uremic pruritus (PMLE is not related to CKD)

data.description: Phototoxic or photoallergic reactions triggered by medications, presenting as pruritic papules, erythema, or eczematous changes confined to sun-exposed areas after UV exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Chronicity in the setting of multiple long-term medications
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of a classic strongly photosensitizing drug in the regimen (no tetracyclines, thiazides, amiodarone, sulfonamides, voriconazole, etc.)
Severe baseline uremic pruritus that can itself cause lesions independent of photosensitivity
Lack of reported acute phototoxic erythema or burning onset after sun exposure

data.description: A variant of lichen planus triggered by sun exposure, presenting with pruritic, flat-topped papules and plaques in sun-exposed areas; more common in spring/summer and in certain skin phototypes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Classic violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules not described
Severe pruritus with sleep impairment is less typical than in prurigo or uremic pruritus
Epidemiology (more typical in younger individuals and certain geographic/ethnic groups) not a perfect fit

http_response.description: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst, initially presenting with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later, she developed acute low back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission she had mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, normal mental status (GCS 15), no fever, and no meningism. Laboratory tests showed mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia. By day 2, she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, decreased temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffmann signs. CSF and electromyography were normal.

data.description: Inflammatory disorder causing acute to subacute dysfunction of the spinal cord, often following a viral prodrome; can present with pain, sensory level, weakness, and autonomic dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Sensory level with decreased temperature sensation below T2/T4
Bilateral Hoffmann signs (upper motor neuron involvement)
Normal EMG (central rather than peripheral process)
Onset days after a possible prodrome (conjunctival hyperaemia, headaches)
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal CSF (CSF is often abnormal but can be normal)
Frontal headaches (non-specific)
Conjunctival hyperaemia (non-specific)
Mild leukocytosis/neutrophilia (not typical but possible with post-infectious states)

data.diagnosis: Anterior spinal artery syndrome (spinal cord ischemia, e.g., fibrocartilaginous embolism)
data.description: Ischemic infarction of the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, often presenting abruptly with severe back pain, weakness, dissociated sensory loss (pain/temperature), and autonomic dysfunction; can occur in adolescents due to fibrocartilaginous embolism.
symptoms_in_common: Dissociated sensory loss with decreased temperature sensation below a thoracic level
Upper motor neuron signs (bilateral Hoffmann signs) as deficits evolve
symptoms_not_in_common: Subacute evolution over several days rather than abrupt onset
Initial left arm pain and headaches (less typical)
Conjunctival hyperaemia (unrelated)
Mild leukocytosis (not expected)
Normal CSF (usually normal in ischemia, but this supports rather than opposes)

data.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis (clinically isolated syndrome with partial myelitis)
data.description: Immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system; in pediatrics, can present with a partial transverse myelitis causing asymmetric weakness and sensory disturbances.
symptoms_in_common: Sensory level with temperature loss (partial myelitis)
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal CSF (oligoclonal bands often present in MS)
Prominent pain (pain can occur but is less dominant in MS myelitis)
Initial conjunctival hyperaemia and headaches (non-specific/prodromal)
Age 15 is compatible but MS often needs dissemination in time/space not yet demonstrated

data.description: An antibody-mediated demyelinating disorder often affecting children; myelitis can be longitudinally extensive, with severe pain, urinary retention, and sometimes normal or mildly abnormal CSF.
symptoms_in_common: Possible normal CSF or mild pleocytosis (normal CSF does not exclude MOGAD)
symptoms_not_in_common: Lack of optic neuritis or encephalitis features (common in MOGAD but not required)
Conjunctival hyperaemia (not typical of MOGAD)
Mild leukocytosis/neutrophilia (non-specific)

data.description: Autoimmune astrocytopathy characterized by severe, often longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and/or optic neuritis; can cause marked pain, sensory loss, weakness, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Acute/subacute myelopathic deficits with sensory level
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 15 (NMOSD is less common in adolescents than adults)
Absence of optic neuritis
Normal CSF (often shows inflammatory changes)
Conjunctival hyperaemia and headaches (non-specific)

data.description: Infection in the epidural space causing back pain and progressive cord compression leading to neurologic deficits and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Acute low back pain worsened by movement
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of fever
Normal CSF (often normal unless meningitis present, but does not localize infection)
Bilateral Hoffmann signs are not specific and cord compression signs may vary
Initial left arm pain, headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia are not typical
Adolescent age makes SEA less common without risk factors

http_response.description: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

data.description: An acute leukemia of immature T-cell precursors that typically presents in adolescents/young adults with high circulating blasts and elevated LDH. Although classically TdT positive, rare cases show TdT negativity while retaining strong T-lineage markers.
symptoms_in_common: Neurologic symptoms (headache, dizziness) and GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting) consistent with hyperleukocytosis/leukostasis
Negative for B- and myeloid markers (CD10/CD19/CD20/CD22/CD13/CD33 negative)
symptoms_not_in_common: TdT negativity (most T-ALL are TdT positive)
Absence of mediastinal mass or lymphadenopathy on exam (often present in T-ALL/T-LBL)
No hepatosplenomegaly (often present)
Hemoglobin 161 g/L (no anemia; anemia is common in acute leukemia)

data.description: An aggressive mature T-cell leukemia of post-thymic T cells characterized by very high leukocyte counts, strong pan–T-cell antigen expression, and TdT negativity. It commonly presents with splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and skin involvement, usually in older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Strong T-cell markers (CD2+, CD3+, CD5+, CD7+)
Neurologic and GI symptoms possibly due to leukostasis
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age (27 years; T-PLL usually affects older adults)
Absence of lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly (commonly present in T-PLL)
Peripheral blood shows 95% blasts (T-PLL typically shows prolymphocytes rather than lymphoblasts)

data.description: A mature T-cell neoplasm driven by HTLV-1 infection, often presenting with leukemic cells expressing mature T markers and TdT negativity. Common features include lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, hypercalcemia, and high LDH; presentations range from indolent to acute leukemic forms.
symptoms_in_common: Mature T-cell immunophenotype (CD3+, CD2+, CD5+, CD7+)
symptoms_not_in_common: No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly (often present)
No reported skin lesions (commonly present)
No hypercalcemia reported (commonly present)
Young age (ATLL more common in older adults, and in HTLV-1 endemic regions)
Peripheral smear with 95% blasts (ATLL cells classically show 'flower' morphology rather than classic lymphoblasts)

data.diagnosis: Hyperleukocytosis with leukostasis secondary to acute T-lineage leukemia
data.description: A life-threatening complication of acute leukemia where very high circulating blast counts increase blood viscosity and impair microvascular perfusion, causing neurologic and respiratory symptoms. Most often seen with acute leukemias and very elevated blast counts.
symptoms_not_in_common: This is a complication rather than a primary leukemia subtype
No respiratory symptoms reported (dyspnea is common in leukostasis)
Hemoglobin normal-high rather than anemic

http_response.description: A 36-year-old Chinese man presented with a 1-month history of persistent fever. He was previously healthy with no significant past medical history, specifically no prior TB infections, chronic illnesses, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, or immune diseases. He was not taking any regular prescription medications and had not travelled abroad. On admission, vital signs showed temperature 37.2°C, heart rate 119 beats/min, blood pressure 90/48 mmHg, respiration rate 38 breaths/min with oxygen saturation 88%. Physical examination revealed an acutely ill appearance and pulmonary rales in both lungs. He presented with persistent fever, pancytopenia, and hyperferritinemia with clinical deterioration including acute respiratory failure.

data.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome due to uncontrolled immune activation, often triggered by infections (e.g., EBV, TB), malignancy, or autoimmune disease; characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, organ dysfunction, and markedly elevated ferritin.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent bilateral pulmonary rales (more typical of primary pneumonia than isolated systemic hyperinflammation)

data.description: A severe lower respiratory tract infection leading to hypoxemic respiratory failure and systemic inflammatory response; ARDS can develop with diffuse alveolar damage and severe hypoxemia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Pancytopenia
Marked hyperferritinemia

data.description: Disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection with hematogenous spread causing systemic symptoms and multi-organ involvement; can cause persistent fever, cytopenias, and respiratory compromise.
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypotension (90/48 mmHg) is less typical unless septic shock develops
Markedly rapid deterioration to severe hypoxemia compared with typical subacute course

data.diagnosis: Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) with possible macrophage activation syndrome
data.description: An autoinflammatory disorder characterized by high spiking fevers, arthralgia, rash, and very high ferritin; can evolve into macrophage activation syndrome (a form of HLH) causing cytopenias and organ failure.
symptoms_not_in_common: Pancytopenia (not typical for uncomplicated AOSD; suggests MAS/HLH)
Prominent bilateral pulmonary rales
Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure
Hypotension (90/48 mmHg)

data.diagnosis: Acute leukemia (e.g., AML/ALL) with secondary infection
data.description: A malignant proliferation of immature hematopoietic cells causing marrow failure (pancytopenia) and infection-related complications; can present with fever and systemic illness.
symptoms_in_common: Hypotension (90/48 mmHg) in setting of sepsis
Acute respiratory failure (often due to concurrent pneumonia/ARDS)
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral pulmonary rales are not a primary feature of leukemia itself (more consistent with superimposed infection)

data.diagnosis: Sepsis of unknown origin with multiorgan dysfunction
data.description: A dysregulated host response to infection leading to life-threatening organ dysfunction and shock; can cause respiratory failure, hypotension, and laboratory abnormalities including cytopenias and elevated ferritin.
symptoms_not_in_common: 1-month duration of fever is longer than typical for acute sepsis prior to decompensation

data.description: SARS-CoV-2 infection causing viral pneumonia and hypoxemic respiratory failure; severe cases can feature a hyperinflammatory state with elevated ferritin and hematologic abnormalities.
symptoms_not_in_common: Pancytopenia (COVID-19 more commonly causes lymphopenia; full pancytopenia is less typical)
Prolonged 1-month febrile course prior to admission is less typical

http_response.description: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.

data.description: Neurologic complications of dengue infection, which can include encephalitis or encephalopathy, occur during or shortly after acute dengue. They are more likely in older adults and can present with fever, altered consciousness, seizures, and focal deficits. Dengue is endemic in many South Pacific islands.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to dengue-endemic South Pacific islands
Transient rash within 48 hours of admission
CSF pleocytosis with predominantly neutrophils (can occur early), elevated protein
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of classic severe dengue warning signs in the history (e.g., plasma leakage, severe thrombocytopenia, hemorrhage), though not always present or reported

data.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus prevalent in parts of Asia-Pacific that causes encephalitis with fever, rapidly progressive altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits; mortality and neurologic sequelae are high in older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to Asia-Pacific region (some visited areas are within broader regional risk zones)
CSF pleocytosis and elevated protein with relatively normal glucose
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient rash (rash is uncommon in Japanese encephalitis)
Predominantly neutrophilic CSF (JE classically shows lymphocytic predominance after the first days, though early neutrophilia can occur)

data.description: A leading cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis in adults, characterized by fever, altered consciousness, focal neurologic signs, and seizures, often with temporal lobe involvement. CSF typically shows elevated protein and pleocytosis; early neutrophilic predominance can occur, with normal glucose.
symptoms_in_common: CSF pleocytosis with possible early neutrophilic predominance
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent tropical travel exposure (not specifically associated with HSV-1)
Transient rash (not typical for HSV-1 encephalitis, unless concurrent mucocutaneous lesions which were not described)

data.description: A foodborne bacterial infection that frequently affects older adults and can cause meningoencephalitis with fever, altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits. CSF may show neutrophilic pleocytosis and elevated protein, with glucose that may be normal or mildly decreased.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced age (81 years, a key risk group)
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient rash (not typical for Listeria meningoencephalitis)
Travel-associated exposure history rather than typical foodborne risk factors (e.g., unpasteurized dairy, deli meats), though exposure history is not provided

data.description: A severe complication of falciparum malaria characterized by impaired consciousness or coma and sometimes focal neurologic signs. It can occur in travelers to malaria-endemic regions and often presents with high fever. CSF may be relatively unremarkable or show mild pleocytosis and protein elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to regions with malaria transmission (e.g., Solomon Islands, Vanuatu)
Focal neurologic deficits can occur in severe cases
CSF that is not profoundly abnormal (mild pleocytosis, elevated protein) and normal glucose
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient rash (rash is not typical of malaria)
No report of periodic fevers, severe anemia, or thrombocytopenia (often present in falciparum malaria)
Neutrophil-predominant CSF (malaria usually doesn’t cause a neutrophilic CSF)

http_response.description: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved on weekly adalimumab over the past 3 years. Presented with 3 weeks of upper respiratory symptoms (sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, chills), followed 2 weeks before presentation by cramping left calf pain and swelling that progressed to the foot, with a purpuric/erythematous rash on the dorsum of both feet. Exam showed left ankle synovitis, intact nasal septum, normal peripheral pulses, and discomfort from left leg pain.

data.description: An IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis often triggered by upper respiratory infections, characterized by palpable purpura on the lower extremities, arthralgias/arthritis, and potential gastrointestinal or renal involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Recent upper respiratory symptoms (sore throat, rhinorrhea, cough, chills) preceding onset
Purpuric erythematous rash on the dorsum of the feet
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked unilateral calf pain and swelling (more suggestive of DVT or localized process)
No reported abdominal pain or renal symptoms (often seen in IgA vasculitis)

data.diagnosis: Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (hypersensitivity vasculitis), possibly anti-TNF–induced
data.description: Immune complex–mediated small-vessel vasculitis of the skin that presents with palpable purpura, often triggered by infections or medications (including TNF inhibitors like adalimumab) and may include arthralgia/arthritis.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable purpuric rash on lower extremities (feet)
Use of adalimumab (a known, though uncommon, trigger)
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent unilateral calf swelling extending to the foot

data.diagnosis: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the left lower extremity
data.description: Formation of a blood clot in a deep vein, commonly presenting with unilateral calf pain and swelling; inflammatory bowel disease is a known hypercoagulable risk state.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral leg swelling progressing to the foot
symptoms_not_in_common: Purpuric rash on both feet (not typical of DVT)
Ankle synovitis
Recent upper respiratory symptoms (not a typical DVT feature)

data.description: A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that can present with palpable purpura, arthralgias, and systemic symptoms; often involves kidneys and lungs, and may be preceded by constitutional or upper airway symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Systemic/upper respiratory symptoms (sore throat, cough, rhinorrhea, chills)
symptoms_not_in_common: Intact nasal septum with no destructive sinonasal disease
No renal or pulmonary manifestations reported
Marked unilateral calf swelling (not a typical primary feature)

data.description: A panniculitis associated with inflammatory bowel disease that presents with tender erythematous nodules on the shins and can be accompanied by arthralgia/arthritis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Purpuric erythematous rash on the dorsum of the feet rather than tender nodules on the shins
Distribution on feet instead of classic anterior shins
Unilateral calf swelling

http_response.description: A 47-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with a six-month history of left-sided sore throat, ipsilateral otalgia, and a six-week history of a left-sided neck mass. He had never smoked and drank less than 5 units of alcohol per week. On examination in the ENT clinic, a firm fixed lymph node was palpable in the upper anterior triangle.

data.diagnosis: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (tonsil/base of tongue)
data.description: A malignancy of the oropharynx, often arising from the palatine tonsil or base of tongue. Frequently HPV-positive, it commonly presents in non-smokers with unilateral sore throat, referred ear pain, and metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Firm, fixed lymph node in upper anterior triangle (level II) consistent with metastatic node

data.description: An Epstein–Barr virus–associated carcinoma arising in the nasopharynx. It often presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and can cause referred ear symptoms and throat discomfort.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral neck mass with firm node
Ipsilateral otalgia (via Eustachian tube dysfunction/referred pain)

data.diagnosis: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to cervical lymph node from occult head and neck primary
data.description: Cervical nodal metastasis from an as-yet unidentified primary tumor in the upper aerodigestive tract; common sites include the oropharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx.
symptoms_in_common: Firm, fixed upper anterior triangle lymph node

data.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving cervical lymph nodes
data.description: A malignant lymphoid neoplasm that can present with painless, firm lymphadenopathy in the cervical region; systemic B symptoms may or may not be present.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral neck mass of several weeks
symptoms_not_in_common: Prolonged unilateral sore throat
Ipsilateral otalgia

data.description: Mycobacterial infection of cervical lymph nodes leading to chronic lymphadenopathy; nodes can be firm and may become matted or fluctuant over time.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prolonged unilateral sore throat
Ipsilateral otalgia

http_response.description: 72-year-old white woman with 10-year history of recurrent cystitis. No systemic symptoms. Physical exam showed slight anemia. Urine cultures were positive for Escherichia coli. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy detected by CT and ultrasound. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and subsequent biopsies were negative for both pathologic lymphoid infiltrate and Helicobacter pylori. Otolaryngologic examination and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Serology for hepatitis C virus and hepatitis B virus was negative. No monoclonal component found in serum protein electrophoresis.

data.diagnosis: Recurrent uncomplicated urinary tract infections due to postmenopausal urogenital atrophy
data.description: Estrogen deficiency after menopause leads to atrophic changes in the vaginal and urethral mucosa, altered vaginal microbiota, and decreased local immunity, predisposing to recurrent bacterial cystitis.
symptoms_in_common: Urine cultures positive for Escherichia coli
symptoms_not_in_common: Slight anemia (not typically caused by uncomplicated recurrent UTIs)
No reported symptoms of vaginal/urethral atrophy (e.g., vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urethral irritation)

data.diagnosis: Diabetes mellitus predisposing to recurrent urinary tract infections
data.description: Chronic hyperglycemia impairs host defenses and promotes glycosuria, fostering bacterial growth and recurrent UTIs, particularly with Enterobacterales such as E. coli.
symptoms_in_common: Urine cultures positive for Escherichia coli
Slight anemia (can be seen with chronic disease or diabetic kidney disease)
symptoms_not_in_common: No systemic symptoms (diabetes often has constitutional or metabolic symptoms when uncontrolled)
No documented hyperglycemia or diabetic complications
No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy is neutral but not explanatory

data.diagnosis: Pelvic organ prolapse with incomplete bladder emptying (cystocele) leading to recurrent UTIs
data.description: Descent of the anterior vaginal wall and bladder (cystocele) can cause urinary stasis and high post-void residuals, predisposing to recurrent bacterial cystitis.
symptoms_in_common: Urine cultures positive for Escherichia coli
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported urinary retention, incomplete emptying, or pelvic pressure/bulge
No urinary incontinence or voiding dysfunction mentioned
Slight anemia (not a typical consequence of cystocele-related UTIs)

data.description: A primary immunodeficiency characterized by low immunoglobulin levels and impaired antibody responses that predispose to recurrent infections; while classically sinopulmonary, recurrent UTIs can occur.
symptoms_in_common: No systemic symptoms such as fevers or weight loss (CVID can present without B symptoms)
symptoms_not_in_common: Urine cultures consistently positive for Escherichia coli (infections in CVID are more often sinopulmonary)
No data on low immunoglobulin levels
Slight anemia is nonspecific
No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy (can be present in CVID-related complications)

data.diagnosis: Indolent lymphoproliferative disorder (e.g., chronic lymphocytic leukemia) considered and unlikely
data.description: CLL and other indolent lymphomas can cause hypogammaglobulinemia and recurrent bacterial infections with anemia, but typically show lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy, or marrow involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy on imaging
Negative bone marrow biopsy
No monoclonal component on serum protein electrophoresis
No systemic symptoms
Urine cultures positive for Escherichia coli (consistent with infection but does not support a primary hematologic etiology in the absence of other findings)

http_response.description: 95-year-old woman admitted after a fall. Medical history includes Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin). Laboratory findings showed elevated white cell count and C reactive protein levels. Urine culture revealed Klebsiella pneumoniae infection. Blood cultures were negative.

data.diagnosis: Acute complicated urinary tract infection (UTI) due to Klebsiella pneumoniae
data.description: Bacterial infection of the urinary tract in a high-risk host (elderly, diabetic), often presenting with systemic inflammatory response; Klebsiella species are common Gram-negative pathogens in older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Urine culture positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent fall

data.description: Infection of the renal parenchyma typically due to ascending bacteria from the lower urinary tract, often causing systemic inflammation and bacteriuria.
symptoms_in_common: Urine culture positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent fall
Blood cultures negative

data.diagnosis: Delirium superimposed on dementia (precipitated by infection)
data.description: Acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition occurring in a patient with baseline dementia, commonly triggered by infections such as UTIs in older adults and often leading to falls.
symptoms_in_common: Alzheimer's disease (baseline cognitive impairment increasing delirium risk)
Evidence of infection/inflammation (elevated WBC and CRP)
Urine culture indicating UTI as a potential precipitant
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood cultures negative

data.description: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection arising from the urinary tract; often associated with systemic inflammatory markers and may or may not have positive blood cultures.
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood cultures negative
Recent fall

data.description: Presence of bacteria in the urine without signs or symptoms of urinary tract infection; common in elderly women and those with diabetes.
symptoms_in_common: Urine culture positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated white cell count
Elevated C-reactive protein
Recent fall

http_response.description: 22-year-old athletic male presented with swelling and locking of the left knee. He had no recent trauma but had several football injuries as a child. Two years prior, he had experienced disabling knee pain.

data.description: A displaced longitudinal meniscal tear (often of the medial meniscus) that can cause mechanical locking and recurrent effusions, frequently related to prior sports injuries.
symptoms_in_common: prior disabling knee pain two years ago
symptoms_not_in_common: no recent trauma (many symptomatic bucket-handle tears present after an acute twist)

data.description: Focal subchondral bone injury (often on the femoral condyle) that can lead to unstable cartilage and intra-articular loose bodies, causing mechanical symptoms and swelling in adolescents and young adults.
symptoms_in_common: prior disabling knee pain two years ago
no recent trauma (symptoms may be insidious)
symptoms_not_in_common: childhood football injuries are not required for this diagnosis

data.description: Irritation or thickening of an embryologic synovial fold that can cause anterior knee pain, snapping, and pseudo-locking, often in active individuals.
symptoms_in_common: swelling of the knee (can occur with irritation)
prior disabling knee pain two years ago
symptoms_not_in_common: true fixed locking is less typical than pseudo-locking
no recent trauma is neutral but plica often presents with activity-related anterior knee pain rather than discrete locking

data.description: Benign metaplastic proliferation of synovium producing multiple cartilaginous loose bodies, leading to chronic swelling, pain, and mechanical locking.
symptoms_not_in_common: age 22 is less typical (usually middle-aged)
history of childhood football injuries is not characteristic
athletic status is not specifically associated

data.diagnosis: Pigmented villonodular synovitis (tenosynovial giant cell tumor)
data.description: Proliferative synovial process causing recurrent monoarticular swelling, stiffness, and sometimes mechanical symptoms due to villonodular tissue or hemosiderin-laden nodules.
symptoms_in_common: chronic course with prior disabling pain
symptoms_not_in_common: history of childhood football injuries is not typical
locking is less common than swelling and stiffness
no recent trauma is neutral but the condition is not trauma-related

data.description: A congenital variant of the lateral meniscus that is thicker and more prone to tearing, causing snapping, locking, and effusions in children and young adults.
symptoms_in_common: history suggestive of long-standing knee issues
symptoms_not_in_common: no recent trauma is neutral
childhood football injuries are not required
symptoms often lateral-specific; side/compartment not specified beyond left knee

http_response.description: 48-year-old male presented with 1-week history of jaundice, dark brown urine, pale stools, and nausea. Medical history and physical exam were unremarkable. Laboratory findings showed hepatic panel in cholestatic pattern: total bilirubin 117 μmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 66.8 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 173 IU/L, γ-Glutamyltransferase 380 IU/L, Alanine transaminase 468 IU/L. CA19-9 was 11783 IU/mL. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and β2-microglobulin were normal.

data.diagnosis: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma (obstructing distal bile duct)
data.description: Malignancy of the pancreatic head that commonly causes distal common bile duct obstruction, leading to painless obstructive jaundice and cholestatic liver enzyme abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Cholestatic liver panel (elevated ALP, GGT, conjugated bilirubin)
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute 1-week onset (pancreatic cancer often evolves over weeks to months)
Absence of weight loss
Absence of abdominal pain or back pain
No palpable gallbladder or other exam findings

data.description: A malignant tumor of the extrahepatic bile ducts that causes biliary obstruction and cholestasis; often associated with markedly elevated CA19-9.
symptoms_in_common: Cholestatic pattern on hepatic panel (elevated ALP, GGT, direct bilirubin)
symptoms_not_in_common: Very short 1-week history (cholangiocarcinoma typically presents more insidiously)
No pruritus reported (common in obstructive cholestasis)
No weight loss or constitutional symptoms reported

data.description: Gallstones within the common bile duct causing obstruction and cholestasis; may present acutely with jaundice and abnormal cholestatic liver tests.
symptoms_in_common: Cholestatic liver enzyme elevation (ALP, GGT) with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Extremely elevated CA19-9 (can rise with obstruction but such high levels are less typical)
Absence of right upper quadrant pain or biliary colic
No history of gallstones or prior biliary disease
ALT markedly elevated (can occur but often less pronounced than cholestatic enzymes)

data.description: Malignancy arising from the gallbladder that can invade or compress the biliary tree, leading to obstructive jaundice and elevated cholestatic enzymes; CA19-9 can be elevated.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very acute 1-week presentation (more often subacute/chronic)
No history of gallstones or chronic cholecystitis
No right upper quadrant mass or tenderness
No weight loss reported

data.diagnosis: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with dominant stricture
data.description: A chronic, immune-mediated cholangiopathy causing multifocal biliary strictures and cholestasis; dominant strictures can acutely obstruct bile flow and raise CA19-9.
symptoms_in_common: Possible elevated CA19-9 with dominant stricture
symptoms_not_in_common: Very high CA19-9 (more suggestive of malignancy than PSC alone)
Acute 1-week onset without prior biliary symptoms
No history of inflammatory bowel disease
Male sex is consistent, but age typically younger and disease is chronic with pruritus

data.diagnosis: Drug-induced cholestasis (e.g., from antibiotics or anabolic steroids)
data.description: Medication-related impairment of bile formation or flow leading to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and cholestatic enzyme elevation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated CA19-9 (can rise with cholestasis but levels >10,000 are unusual)
No reported recent medication exposure
ALT significantly elevated (possible but often less marked in purely cholestatic DILI)
Very acute onset without pruritus
